messages.author: 5276ff4387de2618
messages.subject: Re: Classify an unknown tissue
parts:
Hi Paco,

Thanks for using Cardinal! To predict on a new dataset, you use the predict() method with the trained classifier. So assuming, you've trained a classifier and you call it, say, myClassifier, it would go like, for example:

myDataset <- readMSIData("myFile.extension")
# ... do some pre-processing ... #
myClassifier <- spatialShrunkenCentroids(myDataset, y=myResponse) # or PLS or OPLS
myNewDataset <- readMSIData("myNewFile.extension")
# ... do some pre-processing ... #
myPrediction <- predict(myClassifier, newx=myNewDataset)

Keeping in mind, of course, that the training data and the new data will need to have the same m/z values.

-Kyle

messages.author: 5276ff4387de2618
messages.subject: Re: Classify an unknown tissue
parts:
Hi Edu,

The default is to overlay the probabilities for each class using transparency, but if the probabilities for each class are very close and uncertain, then the image can come out muddled and gray.

Try adding 'mode="classes"' to image() so you have:

image (myPrediction, model=list(r=2, s=12), mode="classes", layout=c(2,1), main="MyPrediction")

which will give the "hard" predictions rather than "soft" predictions.

You can extract the pixel-by-pixel probabilities (and predicted classes) directly with

myPrediction[[r=2, s=12]]$probabilities # predicted probabilities of each class
myPrediction[[r=2, s=12]]$classes # predicted class (highest probability)

to see how close the probabilities are.

Hope this helps.

-Kyle

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: Classify an unknown tissue
parts:
It's optional whether to keep the new X matrix, because -- as you say -- it's not necessary for classification. However, OPLS can also be used as a signal processing technique for removing variation in X that is orthogonal to Y. This step is what makes its coefficients more easily interpretable than ordinary PLS, but it also means it can be useful in some circumstances to have the newly processed X matrix for further downstream analysis.

You can read more about it here:

Trygg, J., & Wold, S. (2002). Orthogonal projections to latent
     structures (O-PLS). Journal of Chemometrics, 16(3), 119-128.
     doi:10.1002/cem.695

(This is also noted in the ?OPLS help page. Relevant papers are cited in the help pages where available.)

-Kylie
